ancient.name: Ain Ghazal 84-1
ancient.story_individual:
AinGhazal 84-1 was discovered in the Ain Ghazal region of Jordan, one of the earliest and continuously occupied sites in the region.

He lived approximately 8,300 years ago in one of the largest Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in the Near East.

His remains were found among a cache of other mixed remains with limited additional information for contextual purposes.

ancient.name: Motz 1
ancient.story_individual:
His remains were found in a flexed position with a fox mandible placed under his cranium. He was an adult at the time of death.

Motz 1 was discovered near the western entrance to the city of Jerusalem about 900 meters from the Tel Motza site.

Motz 1’s remains are approximately 9,300 years old.

ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Michael Hammer
famous.story_individual:
Dr. Michael Hammer is an associate professor and research scientist (Arizona Research Laboratories) at the University of Arizona with joint appointments in anthropology, ecology, and evolutionary biology. Dr. Hammer is a population geneticist who studies patterns of genetic variation in modern-day populations to gain insights into the evolutionary origins of Homo sapiens. 

His pioneering work in sequencing the male inherited Y chromosome led to the industry now known as Genetic Genealogy.

Over the past two decades, Dr. Hammer's research has spanned medical genetics and human population genetics. He has published over 100 articles on subjects including the African origin of human diversity, interbreeding between modern humans and archaic Homo species, and genome diversity in the great apes. In recent years, his team has utilized next-generation sequencing technologies to identify genetic variants causing neurodevelopmental disorders in children.

One of his most notable works includes co-authoring the first paper showing that the Cohanim, a hereditary caste of the Jewish priesthood, descend from a single male ancestor.

Additionally, Dr. Hammer was a leading figure in the Y Chromosome Consortium (YCC), an international body of research groups studying the human Y chromosome. His work with the YCC has played a critical role in advancing our understanding of the Y chromosome and its significance in human evolution, migration patterns, and population history.

Mike Hammer from “Who's Who At FamilyTreeDNA” where he was Chief Scientist and member of the Scientific Advisory Board.

famous.name: Otto the Great
famous.story_individual:
Otto the Great (Otto der Große), also known as Otto I, was Holy Roman Emperor from 962 and King of East Francia from 936, one of the defining rulers of early medieval Europe. He was the son of Henry the Fowler, King of East Francia, and Matilda of Ringelheim, and a member of the Liudolfing, or Ottonian, dynasty. Through his father, Otto inherited the kingship of the East Frankish realm, and through his mother he was connected to the powerful Saxon nobility that helped form the backbone of his rule. This placed him at the center of a dynasty that helped shape the political and religious order of 10th-century Europe.

Crowned king at Aachen in 936, Otto spent much of his reign securing control over the German duchies and strengthening royal authority. He became especially famous for victory over the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, a victory that greatly increased his prestige and established him as the most powerful ruler in central and western Europe. His intervention in Italy and in papal affairs would prove even more important for his later reputation. After crossing south of the Alps to reassert royal authority in Italy and restore Pope John XII in Rome, Otto was crowned Holy Roman Emperor there in 962. That coronation by the pope became the defining moment of his reign, elevating him above the status of a regional king and making him the central political figure in Latin Christendom.

Pictured: Statue of the Magdeburg Rider, thought to be of Otto I. Photographer: Ajepbah; edit: Crisco 1492, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons

His dynastic significance extended far beyond his own lifetime. His marriage to Edith of England, a daughter of King Edward the Elder, linked the Ottonian dynasty to the royal house of Anglo-Saxon England, while his descendants remained central to imperial politics for generations. The Ottonian house continued to occupy a leading position in imperial politics after his death.

Genetic research is adding another dimension to our understanding of Otto’s life and identity. Analysis of Otto’s remains from Magdeburg Cathedral has shown that Otto belonged to Y-DNA haplogroup R-FTA63331, a paternal lineage so far observed only rarely in present-day testers, including single representatives from Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, and South Africa. His maternal haplogroup is K1a4a1a2b, likewise a lineage associated primarily with northwest Europe. Genetic sequencing was carried out by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, while Y-chromosomal and mitochondrial DNA analysis was performed by FamilyTreeDNA. The identification of Otto’s remains was also supported by comparison with his great-nephew Saint Henry, whose sequenced remains showed the expected autosomal relationship and carried the same Y-DNA lineage.

Reference

  • Ringbauer, H., Wozniak, T., Feuchter, J., Runfeldt, G., Bianco, R. A., Zhang, G., Prüfer, K., Orschiedt, J., Simm, A., Maier, P., Sager, M., Dresely, V., Krause, J., Meller, H., & Wehner, D. (2026). Reconstructing their genomes confirms the historically attested genealogy of the two medieval emperors Otto I (“the Great”) and Heinrich II (“Saint Henry”). bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.18.712637

Pictured: Seal of Otto I, from The Seals of the German Emperors and Kings: Volume 5:Page 12, No. 5. Otto Posse, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

famous.name: Schinderhannes
famous.story_individual:
For two centuries, the skeletons of criminals, Johannes Bückler, better known as Schinderhannes and his sidekick, Hölzerlips, have been misidentified. These skeletons have been displayed in the Anatomical Collection at Heidelberg University in Germany for two centuries.

Schinderhannes terrorized the German countryside around Mainz in the late 1790s and early 1800s and was accused of at least 211 crimes when he was arrested in 1802. In 1799, he had met Christian Reinhard known as Schwarzer Jonas, another professional criminal. While they teamed up to commit crimes, they also fought, with Jonas breaking Schinderhannes’ arm during one of their arguments.

In November of 1803, following a lengthy trial, attended by a large audience, Schinderhannes, Hölzerlips, Jonas and 17 others were executed by guillotine. 30,000 people attended the spectacle. Their heads were collected into a sack, and their bodies were collected behind a flap and were placed into prepared coffins. Most of the bodies were then made available to scientific groups for research purposes.

In 1805, Fidelis Ackermann, the first chair for Anatomy at Heidelberg University brought his collection of teaching materials along with him from Mainz which included two human skeletons, identified as “natürliches Scelet des Schwarzen Jonas, No. 2“ (the natural skeleton of Schwarzer Jonas, number 2) and “natürliches Scelet des Schinder-Hannes, No. 3“ (the natural skeleton of Schinderhannes, number 3. After Ackermann’s death, his items were merged with the university collection, and the skulls of Schinderhannes and Jonas were loaned to the Anatomy Department in Frankfurt to be drawn, but their whereabouts after that are not documented.

In 1971, a newspaper reported that the bones of Hölzerlips, a robber executed by sword along with three other robbers in Heidelberg in 1812, had not been exhibited for a long time. It was also unclear where the skeleton of Jonas was kept at that, inferring that a mix-up of the skeletons may have taken place.

In 2009, additional questions arose about the correct identification of the remains. Based upon a number stamped on the pelvis of one of the skeletons, the skeleton assigned to Hölzerlips could have been Schwarzer Jonas, another criminal who was executed at the same time.

An exhaustive interdisciplinary investigation was launched.

Researching the documentation retained at the Institute of Heidelberg about the history of the skeletons revealed that the collection numbers assigned to "Schwarzer Jonas" and "Schinderhannes" had been repeatedly changed.

In addition to isotope, anthropological and radiological analyses, DNA was taken from teeth, ribs and a sample from their femurs. Since the skulls had been separated from the bodies, both initially and later when loaned for drawing, there was no certainty that the correct head had been reunited with the appropriate torso.

A maternal pedigree was created using baptismal registers, and a DNA sample was collected from a maternal descendant of Schinderhannes’ mother

Mitochondrial DNA analysis of the skeletons confirm that the correct skulls had been reunited with their respective torsos.

Analysis of Schinderhannes and his maternal fourth cousin excludes the originally labeled skeleton as his. DNA results combined with other data confirm that indeed, the skeletons were confused, and that Schinderhannes was the skeleton previously attributed to Hölzerlips and later to Schwarzer Jonas. However, the identity of the skeleton originally attributed to Schinderhannes remains unknown.

Reference

  • Parson, W., Alterauge, A., Amory, C., Heinze, S., Hölzl, S., Jahn, R. G., Lehn, C., Sänger, T., Xavier, C., Tillmar, A., Nolte, K., Lutz-Bonengel, S., & Doll, S. (2025). Remains of the German outlaw Johannes Bückler alias Schinderhannes identified by an interdisciplinary approach. Forensic Science International: Genetics, 103276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2025.103276

Pictured: Portrait of Schinderhannes (1803) by Karl Matthias Ernst (1758-1830), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

famous.name: John Barber "The Griswold Vampire"
famous.story_individual:
In mid-19th century New England, in Griswold, Connecticut, the Ray farming family was suffering multiple deaths from tuberculosis (then known as consumption). The effects of this contagious disease typically include pale skin, red and swollen eyes, blood around the mouth from coughing, and the general appearance of the infected person slowly “wasting away.”

As the family saw their members waste away in this way over a period of nine years, superstitious beliefs eventually set in. They concluded that they were being consumed by the undead. To protect themselves, they disinterred their dead relatives and burned them. This caused the Ray family to become known as the Jewett City vampires.

The Walton Family Cemetery was rediscovered in the early 1990s as some children were playing near a mine in Jewett City and came across the unmarked graveyard. The graves were found to belong to both the Walton and Ray families.

One grave was found to have a body that had been buried, exhumed, and reburied with the skull dislocated from the spine and buried face down on top of the femurs, which were placed in a “skull and crossbones” formation. An examination of the skeleton showed that the person had suffered from tuberculosis. The dismemberment of the body is thought to have been an attempt to “kill the vampire” and stop him from haunting the living relatives.

The identity of the person was not known, but the coffin had “JB55” inscribed on the lid with brass tacks. Neighboring graves had similar markings. The coffin of an adolescent boy was marked “NB13“ and that of an adult female was marked “IB.“ These markings are thought to represent the deceased’s initials and age at death.

Jennifer Daniels-Higginbotham et al. DNA tested the remains and published the conclusions from the study in the 2019 paper “DNA Testing Reveals the Putative Identity of JB55, a 19th Century Vampire Buried in Griswold, Connecticut.”

Using Y-STR testing, they determined that JB55 and NB13 had the same Y-DNA signature, suggesting that they could be close patrilineal relatives. Assuming that the “B” was the initial for the family surname, they looked in the public FamilyTreeDNA R1b Project and found two identical matches with the surname Barber:

A search of historical records led to a death notice mentioning John Barber, whose son Nathan Barber was buried in Griswold in 1826. The description of Nathan Barber closely fits the burial of “NB13,” found near JB55. By applying modern forensic DNA tools to a historical mystery, the identity of JB55 as John Barber, the 19th century Connecticut vampire, has been revealed.

Historical information source from Wikipedia and Jennifer Daniels-Higginbotham et al. 2019. Pictures courtesy of Connecticut State Archaeologist Nicholas Bellantoni. Coffin lid photo was modified for visibility.

famous.name: Blue Fugate family
famous.story_individual:
Elizabeth Smith and her husband, Martin Fugate, are progenitors of the Blue Fugate Family of Troublesome Creek, in Hazard County, Kentucky.

Elizabeth’s descendants were known as “The Blue Fugates” and also “The Blue People of Kentucky” because some of her children carried a recessive autosomal genetic trait that predisposed them to the blood disorder Methemoglobinemia. While Elizabeth Smith is one of the female progenitors of this cluster of blue-hued people, so is her sister, Mary Smith. Both Smith sisters married Fugate men, and both couples had blue children.

Methemoglobinemia causes the skin to appear blue due to an oxygen deficiency in the red blood cells. Some people only exhibit this characteristic, or even just blue tinges in their fingernails and lips, when they are cold or agitated, such as when infants cry.

At high levels, Methemoglobinemia can cause health issues, but at lower levels, the only symptom is blue skin.

Of Elizabeth’s 11 known children, 4 were noticeably “blue” and lived long, healthy lives.

For Elizabeth and Mary’s children to exhibit blue skin, they would have had to inherit a copy of the gene from both parents, so we know that Elizabeth’s husband, Martin Fugate and Mary’s husband Zachariah also inherited the mutation from one of their parents.

In the 1960s, hematologist Madison Cawein III, with the assistance of Ruth Pendergrass, studied 189 members of the extended Fugate family, treated their symptoms, and published his findings in the Archives of Internal Medicine.

Later, geneticist Ricky Lewis wrote about the Blue Fugates, sharing among other things, the provenance of that “blue” family photo that circulates on the internet, revealing that it is a composite that was assembled and colorized back in 1982.

Earlier research and studies suffered from same-name confusion, reporting that Martin Fugate and Elizabeth Smith’s youngest son, Zachariah Fugate (born in 1871), married his mother’s sister (born about 1820), and had a family. That’s incorrect, or course. The Zachariah Fugate who married Elizabeth Smith’s sister, Mary Smith, was Martin’s second cousin by that same name.

Both Elizabeth Smith and Mary Smith had blue children with their respective Fugate husbands, which helps cement the fact that the responsible genes were passed down through both the Fugate and Smith lines, and weren’t just random mutations or caused by environmental or other factors.

We don’t know a lot about Elizabeth and Mary Smith’s ancestors back in Virginia, but we do know that three generations of their matrilineal ancestors and their families crossed the Appalachian Mountains at Pound Gap and found their way to Perry County, Kentucky, where they set up housekeeping on Fugate’s Fork of Troublesome Creek in the 1830s and 1840s.

Both Elizabeth Smith and her sister, Mary Smith, who married Fugate men, were progenitors of the Blue Fugate family of Kentucky through their parents, Richard Smith and Nancy Eletia Combs.

Further reading: DNAeXplained - The Mystery of the Blue Fugates and Smiths: A Study in Blue Genes and Pedigree Collapse.

Sources include WikiTree, Wikipedia, The Blue People of Troublesome Creek, Fugates of Kentucky: Skin Bluer than Lake Louise, Those Old Kentucky Blues: An Interrupted Case Study, and Finding the Famous Paintings of the Blue People of Kentucky and the Fugate DNA Project.

Sources include WikiTree, Wikipedia, The Blue People of Troublesome Creek, Fugates of Kentucky: Skin Bluer than Lake Louise, Those Old Kentucky Blues: An Interrupted Case Study, and Finding the Famous Paintings of the Blue People of Kentucky and the Fugate DNA Project.

Photo is Luna Fugate (1887-1964) who descended from both couples and is considered to be the bluest of the Blue Fugates. Source: WikiTree.

famous.name: Craig Venter
famous.story_individual:
John Craig Venter, a leading biochemist, was an American businessman and entrepreneur. Listed among Time Magazine’s 100 Most Influential People in the World. Venter is best known for funding the Human Genome Project, where he shared credit for sequencing the human genome.

In 2007, Venter, along with a team led by Sam Levy, sequenced and released Venter’s own partial genome, one of the first made public, which is available today for all researchers to utilize.

Venter founded the J. Craig Venter Institute and Human Longevity, which focused on extending the healthy human lifespan.

Information sourced from the J. Craig Venter Institute, Wikipedia, Nature Journal, Time, Harvard Business Review.

famous.name: Maggie Gyllenhaal
famous.story_individual:
Margaret "Maggie" Ruth Gyllenhaal was born on November 16, 1977, in New York City, and her brother, Jake, arrived on December 19, 1980. Their mother, Naomi Foner, established herself as a respected screenwriter in Hollywood, earning an Oscar nomination for "Running on Empty" (1988). The family's Jewish heritage comes through Foner's line, as her grandparents were Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants who left Eastern Europe (specifically Latvia and Poland) for America.

Maggie's maternal ancestry was documented when she appeared on PBS's "Finding Your Roots" (Season 1, Episode 6). The DNA testing conducted for the show revealed that she belongs to mitochondrial haplogroup K1a1b1a, a genetic lineage that is common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. This haplogroup, passed down through the maternal line, provides a direct genetic link to her Eastern European Jewish ancestors.

In her professional life, Maggie first drew critical attention with her performance in "Secretary" (2002), followed by notable roles in films such as "Sherrybaby" (2006) and "The Dark Knight" (2008). She later moved into directing, making her debut with "The Lost Daughter" (2021), which earned multiple award nominations. Her brother Jake has similarly built an acclaimed acting career, with standout performances in films such as "Brokeback Mountain" (2005), "Zodiac" (2007), and "Nightcrawler" (2014).

While the siblings carry the Swedish surname Gyllenhaal from their father, Stephen, a film director, their maternal heritage traces to their great-grandmother, Yetta Silbowitz (née Sklar, 1890-1960), who emigrated from Latvia.

Photo: Maggie Gyllenhaal at Berlinale 2017. Maximilian Bühn, CC-BY-SA 4.0, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Thuya
famous.story_individual:
Thuya was a prominent noblewoman in the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. She held several prestigious titles including "Singer of Hathor" and "Chief of the Entertainers," indicating her significant role in religious and court life.

She married Yuya, a powerful adviser to Pharaoh Amenhotep III, and together they became one of the most influential couples of their time. Their daughter Tiye went on to become the Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III, elevating the family's status even further. Through Tiye, Thuya became the great-grandmother of the famous pharaoh Tutankhamun.

Thuya was buried alongside her husband Yuya in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes. Their tomb (KV46) was discovered in 1905 and was remarkably well-preserved, being one of the few non-royal tombs in the valley. The mummies of both Thuya and Yuya were found in excellent condition, allowing for later DNA analysis.

Modern genetic studies, including those conducted by Zahi Hawass et al. in 2010, confirmed Thuya's biological relationship to several members of the royal family. The DNA analysis proved that she was indeed the grandmother of both Akhenaten and The Younger Lady (KV35YL), who were the parents of Tutankhamun.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

The same studies revealed that Thuya lived to be around 50-60 years old, based on examination of her mummy. Her preserved remains show she had long, wavy white hair, and she appears to have been treated with the highest respect in death, as evidenced by the quality of her mummification and burial goods.

famous.name: Yuya
famous.story_individual:
Yuya was a powerful man in the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. He served as a key adviser for Amenhotep III and carried many titles such as "King’s Lieutenant" and "Master of the Horse."

He married the Egyptian noblewoman Thuya and was the great-grandfather of Tutankhamun through their daughter Tiye, who was the Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III, the ninth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

Because of the many different spelling variants of his name and his physical features, some Egyptologists have speculated that he had foreign origins.

Yuya and his wife were buried in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes.

Zahi Hawass et al. 2010 studied the DNA of 11 royal mummies of the New Kingdom to determine their familial relationships and medical conditions. They studied Yuya and his wife Thuya, their daughter Tiye, and their grandchildren Abhenaten and The Younger Lady (KV35YL) and determined that their grandchildren were the full sibling parents of Tutankhamun.

Gad et al. 2020 further elaborated on the Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family and provided the haplogroup estimates based on DNA-tested Y-STR markers in the mummy remains. Please note that the haplogroup assignment is based on a small number of Y-STR markers as published in the paper. Further DNA testing and analysis may provide updates to the haplogroup assignments.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

Historical information sourced from Wikipedia. Pictured: Mummy mask of Yuya. Photo credit: Jon Bodsworth

famous.name: Tutankhamun
famous.story_individual:
Tutankhamun or King Tut was the last pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. He ruled the New Kingdom from a very young age, becoming a pharaoh at the age of 8 or 9. His reign was short, and he died young at around 18 years old without any heirs, ending the dynasty.

He was buried in the Valley of the Kings and became the most well-recognized symbol of ancient Egypt after his entirely complete and nearly-intact tomb was discovered in 1922. It was the first royal tomb discovered in Egypt that had not been looted by grave robbers. His two infant daughters were also buried in his tomb.

Archaeologist and Egyptologist Howard Carter opens the innermost shrine of King Tutankhamun's tomb (1925)

Zahi Hawass et al. 2010 studied the DNA of 11 royal mummies of the New Kingdom to determine their familial relationships and medical conditions. They studied Tutankhamun and determined that his parents were full siblings and that the unknown mummy KV55 was Tut’s father. They further identified the father as Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV), but this identification has been questioned and said to be uncertain.

Tut’s grandfather, identified as Amenhotep III, shared his paternal lineage, which genealogically traces back to Thutmose I the third pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty. His great-grandparents on his grandmother Tiye’s side were identified as Yuya and Thuya.

Gad et al. 2020 further elaborated on the Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family and provided the haplogroup estimates based on DNA-tested Y-STR markers in the mummy remains. Please note that the haplogroup assignment is based on a small number of Y-STR markers as published in the paper. Further DNA testing and analysis may provide updates to the haplogroup assignments.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

A painted, wooden figure of Tutankhamun found in his royal tomb

Pictured: The funerary mask of Tutankhamun, Roland Unger, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Historical information sourced from Wikipedia.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
